Fleet services manages and maintains the civic fleet and a cost recovery model.

Tailgate slamming from trucks unloading snowed the civic operation center at snow management facility has been a concern for the residents of Montgomery place.
In May 2022, the administration reported to the Standing Policy Committee on Transportation on Tailgate slamming concerns received in the 2021 and 2021-22 interseasons.
The report included additional improvements planned for implementation as well as a commitment to collect noise data originating from the COC site in the 2022-23 interseasons.
As per the commitment, an environmental noise study within Montgomery place was completed by consultant between 39 and March 3rd, 2023.
The study was completed during the activation of the Rovis Emergency Response Plan, collection of noise data coincided with peak activity at the COC 1 and 2 sites.
This report provides a summary of the collected noise data and findings of the study.
Noise data was collected using three noise monitoring stations set up in the south east, south and south west parts of Montgomery place.
The noise levels at the south east monitoring station were dominated by road noise on circle drive and real activity.
Snow pushing equipment operating at the COC 1 and 2 sites, including the engine noise and backup alarms, were inaudible on the recorded audio.

The noise levels at the south monitoring station were dominated by rail activity, noise from the COC 1 and 2 sites were audible at the monitoring location during periods of low or no rail activity nearby.
The noise levels at the south west monitoring station were largely determined by rail related activity followed by the activity at the COC 1 and 2 sites.
Noise from the COC 1 and 2 sites was audible at the monitoring location during periods of low or no rail activity nearby.

The maximum noise levels associated with occasional tailgate slams and sledgehammer banks on truck boxes were audible on the recorded audio at all three monitoring locations, but below the noise levels associated with rail activity.
The noise levels and frequency of occurrence associated with tailgate slams and sledgehammer banks were not high enough to affect the overall monitored noise levels.
For normal operations, rail-related activity is the dominant noise source, but there is contribution from the COC1 and two operations.
On June 6, 2023, the administration presented a summary of the noise study findings to the Montgomery Police Community Association.

Tailgate slaming mitigation, engine retarder brake retarder brake signage, and creation of additional permanent snow storage sites were identified as mitigation priorities for the Montgomery Police neighborhood.
Unless otherwise directed, the administration will undertake the following steps.
The planning and development department will prepare an implementation plan to increase enforcement of engine retarder brake regulations and assess traffic volumes and circle guides south.
The robust feet and support department will continue to educate snow haulers and raise awareness about the impacts of tailgate slaming annually at the start of the snow hauling season.
Two, prohibit tailgate slaming and amended the use of non-stick material contract pets for city-owned or control trucks.
Three, provide on-site monitoring of city-owned or control equipment to ensure it is equipped with appropriately sized exhaust sensors.
Four, use snow to construct noise berms where and when possible.
And five, work with other city departments to identify and develop additional permanent snow storage sites subject to available funding.

Good afternoon, Mr. Chair and committee members. Again, my name is Jamie Agust. I'm the Director of Transportation with the here at the city.

The administration frequently receives inquiries from care homes, schools, government and businesses to include an accessible ramp for the loading zones in front of their facilities to accommodate people using mobility devices.
Typically an accessible ramp refers to a change in the grade of the sidewalk to match the driving surface.
There by eliminating the curb facing allowing mobility devices to move from the driving surface to the sidewalk more easily.
The city of Saskatoon currently has no guidelines as to the geometry of the accessible accessibility ramps at suggested locations such as these.

To that end, the administration in collaboration with some community partners plans on completing a one year pilot project regarding the installation of accessibility ramps for loading zones at three locations to review and confirm some design standards for the following three scenarios.
A combined carbon sidewalk, a separate carbon sidewalk in a wide sidewalk, such as downtown.
Appendix two of the report includes some preliminary draft design standards and they include the following features.
Longer loading zone dimensions to accommodate loading requirements from a rear loading vehicle access aisles to accommodate loading requirements from a side loading vehicle.
A clear width platform so that loading activities would not obstruct the sidewalk.
Maximum slope and grade requirements to accommodate the use of mobility devices.
The pilot project will include a monitoring program and stakeholder engagement.
The monitoring program has been structured to capture information about the project that will help inform the administration.
Specifically, we'll consider and look at ponding street sweeping, snow clearing and accessible ramp geometrics.
The preliminary engagement stakeholder team has been identified and includes people from Saskabilities, Saskatoon Council on Aging, the downtown and event and entertainment district.

The bids, southernland school, Saskatoon public school division, sturdy stone center, Luther special care center, roadways and fleet department, water and waste operation at the department community standards, specifically the parking services.
The active transportation advisory group and the low vision community CNIB or AAPC.
If this report is forwarded to the accessibility advisory committee of council, we look forward to potentially also receiving feedback from that committee.
The three locations where the pilot project will be implemented are Luther special care home, southernland elementary school and the sturdy stone building.
The owners of these buildings have previously requested the installation of ramps for their clients that use mobility devices.
Representatives from all three locations have agreed to fund the installations and are also committed to assist in the monitoring and engagement requirements of the pilot project.
We like to thank these community partners.

Upon success of the pilot project, the administration will prepare and propose an accessible loading zone policy to city council that would provide guidance and regulation regarding the installation of accessibility ramps and other features moving forward.
